info.name: toy-mcp
info.description:
Requests for the two toy MCP servers of the toy-mcp repository: a server built on v1 of the official TypeScript SDK, for protocol 2025-11-25, and a hand-written server for protocol 2026-07-28. One folder per server.

Start the server a folder talks to before sending its requests, from the repository root:

- `npm start` for the SDK server, at `http://127.0.0.1:3333/mcp`
- `npm run start:2026` for the hand-written server, at `http://127.0.0.1:3334/mcp`

The collection variables `sdk` and `s2026` hold those two URLs. If you start a server on another port (for example `PORT=4000 npm start`), change the matching variable. The third variable, `jobId`, is set by the script on the `start_job` request; if it stays empty, paste the `jobId` from a `start_job` reply into it.

Send the requests of a folder from top to bottom. Each name ends with what to expect: the HTTP status and, for a failure, the JSON-RPC error code or `isError`. No environment and no authorization are needed.

item.name: SDK server :3333 (protocol 2025-11-25)
item.description:
Version 1 of the official TypeScript SDK (`@modelcontextprotocol/sdk`) in stateless mode. Start it with `npm start`.

Every reply in this folder is HTTP 200 with an SSE frame, even for a single response: the JSON-RPC message is on the `data:` line. A problem with a tool call comes back as a result with `isError: true`. A problem with the protocol comes back as a JSON-RPC `error`.

Both headers are required. The SDK answers 406 without `Accept: application/json, text/event-stream` and 415 without `Content-Type: application/json`.

request.description: The handshake of the 2025 protocol. The reply carries `protocolVersion`, `capabilities` and `serverInfo`. No `Mcp-Session-Id` response header comes back, because the server runs in stateless mode.
Lists the five tools with the JSON Schema of their inputs. It works without a prior `initialize`, because the server keeps no session.
The minimal tool call. The result is an array of typed content blocks, here one text block holding `hello`.
`text` is a number. The SDK validates the arguments before the tool runs and answers with a normal result marked `isError: true`. The text names the failing field (`at text`).
A tool that does not exist. The answer has the same shape as a validation failure: a result with `isError: true` (`Tool nope not found`), not a JSON-RPC error.
Step one of the marketplace pattern: find out what exists. An empty `query` returns all three items with their price and input fields. Set `query` to `report` to narrow it to one item.
Step two of the marketplace pattern: one generic tool runs any item. The reply shows the input after defaults were applied (`maxResults: 10`) and the price charged.

item.name: call_item - two bad fields named -> 200 isError

request.description: A bad enum value and a number out of range. Both fields are named in one reply (`input.mode` and `input.maxResults`), so a caller can fix the whole input in one retry.

exec: // The reply is an SSE frame. The JSON-RPC message is on the data: line, and the tool's
// answer is a JSON string inside result.content[0].text.

request.description:
Starts a long-running item and returns a `jobId` handle instead of holding a session open. Send it twice: the second reply carries the same `jobId` with `deduplicated: true`, because the `idempotencyKey` is the same.

The script on this request copies the `jobId` into the `jobId` collection variable for `get_result`. The server remembers a key until it restarts, so a first reply that already says `deduplicated: true` means `k-1` was used earlier.
`maxCostUsd` is below the price of the item (0.01 USD), so the job is refused before any work starts.

Reads a job by its handle, taken from the `jobId` collection variable. For three seconds after `start_job` the state is `running`; after that it is `succeeded` and carries the result.

An empty or unknown `jobId` gets `No job ...` with `isError: true`. A valid id gets the same answer after the server restarts, because jobs live in memory.

The method that replaces `initialize` in the 2026-07-28 revision. Version 1 of the SDK does not implement that revision and answers with the JSON-RPC error `-32601` inside an HTTP 200. Compare request A in the other folder, where the same method is answered, and request H, where an unknown method is an HTTP 404.

item.name: confirm_purchase - no session, cannot ask -> 200 isError

request.description:
The tool needs the user to confirm, but on the stateless route the server cannot ask. Each request gets a fresh server that never saw `initialize`, so it does not know whether the client can answer a question, and the answer would arrive at yet another fresh server anyway. The result is a tool failure: `Could not ask the user: ...`.

The session folder shows the same call succeeding.

item.name: SDK server :3333, session mode (/mcp-session)
item.description: The same SDK server on a second route that keeps a session per client. Send the requests in order. Request 4 stays open until request 7 answers it, so send 5, 6 and 7 from other tabs while 4 is waiting. The server waits two minutes for an answer.

request.description:
Opens a session. The reply carries an `Mcp-Session-Id` response header; a script stores it in the `sessionId` collection variable, and every later request in this folder sends it.

`capabilities.elicitation` tells the server that this client can show a form and send back the answer. The server remembers it for the whole session, which is why it may ask later.

Behind the id the server keeps one server object and one transport in memory until the session ends.
An ordinary request inside the session. The `Mcp-Session-Id` header routes it to the server object that request 1 created.
On this route every request after `initialize` must carry the session id. Without it the server cannot tell which session the request belongs to.

The tool asks the user to confirm the price before it charges. The response is an SSE stream that stays open. Its first message is a request from the server to the client: `elicitation/create`, with the question and the form to fill in. Note its `id`.

Leave this tab waiting and send requests 5, 6 and 7 from other tabs. When 7 is accepted, the tool result arrives here as a second message and the stream ends.

This is the server-to-client direction that needs a session: the answer is a separate HTTP request, and only the session id connects it to this waiting call.

The answer to the question, sent without `Mcp-Session-Id`. The server refuses it: it cannot know which session, and so which waiting tool call, the answer is for. Request 4 keeps waiting.

The body is a JSON-RPC response, not a request: it has `result` and no `method`. Its `id` must equal the `id` of the `elicitation/create` message in the stream of request 4. That is `0` for the first question in a session and goes up by one for each further question.

item.name: 6  answer sent to the stateless route (dropped) -> 202

request.description:
The same answer sent to `/mcp`. The reply is `202 Accepted`, yet nothing happens: the request reached a fresh server with no tool call waiting, so the answer is dropped without an error. Request 4 keeps waiting.

This is what happens behind a load balancer when the answer reaches a process that does not hold the session.

The body is a JSON-RPC response, not a request: it has `result` and no `method`. Its `id` must equal the `id` of the `elicitation/create` message in the stream of request 4. That is `0` for the first question in a session and goes up by one for each further question.

The answer, with the session id. The server accepts it with `202` and no body, hands it to the waiting tool call, and request 4 finishes with `purchased: true`.

Change `confirm` to `false`, or `action` to `decline`, and the tool finishes with `purchased: false`.

The body is a JSON-RPC response, not a request: it has `result` and no `method`. Its `id` must equal the `id` of the `elicitation/create` message in the stream of request 4. That is `0` for the first question in a session and goes up by one for each further question.
Ends the session. The server drops the server object and the transport it kept for this id.
The id no longer names a session. `404` tells a client to start again with `initialize`. A server restart has the same effect, because sessions live in memory.

item.name: Hand-written server :3334 (protocol 2026-07-28)
item.description:
Node's `http` module only, for the 2026-07-28 revision. Start it with `npm run start:2026`. JSON-RPC replies are plain JSON, not SSE frames.

A is the valid request. B to L are each answered with an error, and the name ends with the HTTP status and, where there is one, the JSON-RPC error code that comes back.

A valid request carries the `MCP-Protocol-Version` and `Mcp-Method` headers (plus `Mcp-Name` for `tools/call`, `resources/read` and `prompts/get`), and `params._meta` with the protocol version and the client capabilities.

request.description: The discovery call that replaces the `initialize` handshake. The reply lists `supportedVersions` and `capabilities`, names the server under `_meta`, and carries `ttlMs` and `cacheScope` so a client can cache it.

item.name: B  discover - no MCP headers, no params -> 400 -32020

request.description: Only `Content-Type` and `Accept` are sent: no `MCP-Protocol-Version` header, no `Mcp-Method` header and no `params`. The header check runs first, so the answer is `-32020` and not the `-32602` of request C.
The headers are right but `params._meta` is missing. That is a malformed request: `-32602`.
The header says `2025-11-25` and `_meta` says `2026-07-28`. The request contradicts itself: `-32020`.
The header and `_meta` agree on a version the server does not speak. `error.data` lists `supported` and `requested`, so a client knows what to retry with.
The `Mcp-Method` header says `tools/list` and the body says `server/discover`: `-32020`.
For `tools/call` the `Mcp-Name` header must equal `params.name`. Here the header says `foo` and the body says `bar`: `-32020`.
A method the spec defines but this server does not implement. Its headers and `_meta` are valid, so it passes every per-request rule and only then gets `404` with `-32601`.
What a 2025 client sends first. The handshake was removed in this revision, so the server answers `-32022` and lists the versions it supports in `error.data`.
The body is valid JSON but not an object, so it is not a JSON-RPC request: `-32600` with `id: null`.
The body cannot be parsed as JSON at all: `-32700` with `id: null`.

The 2026-07-28 revision removed the standalone GET stream, so `GET` on the endpoint is answered with HTTP 405. This server sends 405 with an `Allow: POST` header and an empty body for every method other than POST.

Lists the tools. Each one has a `name`, a `description` and an `inputSchema` in JSON Schema. The result also carries `resultType`, plus `ttlMs` and `cacheScope` so a client or a shared cache can reuse the list.
A successful call. The `Mcp-Name` header repeats `params.name`. The result has `resultType: "complete"` and a `content` array, and no `isError`.
Runs a catalog item. The reply shows `ranWith` with the default `maxResults: 10` applied, and `chargedUsd`.

item.name: P  tools/call call_item - two bad fields -> 200 isError

request.description: A tool failure, not a protocol failure: HTTP 200 and a normal result with `isError: true`. The text names both failing fields, so the caller can fix the whole input in one retry.

A protocol failure: the tool does not exist, so the reply is a JSON-RPC error with `-32602`. Compare with P, where the tool exists and its failure is a result. The SDK server answers the same request with an `isError` result.

exec: // The reply is plain JSON here (the SDK server answers with an SSE frame). The tool's answer
// is a JSON string inside result.content[0].text.

request.description:
The same tool, from the same definition, as in the SDK server. It returns a `jobId` handle and the request ends; nothing is held open. Send it twice: the second reply carries the same `jobId` with `deduplicated: true`.

The script on this request copies the `jobId` into the `jobId2026` collection variable for T. The two servers have separate job stores, so each has its own variable.

item.name: S  tools/call start_job - over budget -> 200 isError

request.description: `maxCostUsd` is below the price of the item (0.01 USD), so the job is refused before any work starts. A tool failure: HTTP 200 and a result with `isError: true`.

Reads the job started in R. This is a separate request with no session and no `initialize`: the `jobId` is all the server needs. The state is `running`, then `succeeded` after about three seconds.

If it answers `No job`, send R first: the variable is empty, or the server was restarted and its in-memory jobs are gone.

item.name: U  tools/call confirm_purchase (cannot ask yet) -> 200 isError

request.description: The tool needs the user to confirm, and this server cannot ask yet. This revision has no session to carry a question, so it uses a multi round-trip request instead: an `input_required` result that the client answers by sending the request again. That is step 5. Until then the call is a tool failure.
